claims.text: Controlled elemental segregation induced during processing forms a uniform nanoscale passivation oxide layer.
The nanoscale passivation oxide layer reinforces the alloy microstructure.
The passivation oxide layer protects the alloy against corrosion and high-temperature oxidation.
Segregation-controlled passivation enables lightweight HEAs to combine low density, high strength, corrosion resistance, and oxidation resistance.
Standard processing of an AlCrTiV0.5 baseline produces moderate elemental segregation.
Standard processing of the baseline produces incomplete passivation-film formation.
Cooling rate and heat-treatment protocols can tune the degree of elemental segregation.
Rapid quenching or heavy rolling can disrupt beneficial nanoscale segregation.
Chemically coherent segregation of minor alloying elements facilitates formation of a uniform, adherent oxide layer along grain boundaries and within the matrix.
Controlled segregation induces microstructural refinement that promotes strengthening.
Disrupted segregation produces heterogeneous oxide films and a less optimized microstructure.
Relative to the baseline, controlled segregation will produce a more uniform and adherent nanoscale passivation layer.
Relative to the baseline, controlled segregation will increase tensile and yield strengths.
Relative to the baseline, controlled segregation will improve corrosion resistance.
Relative to the baseline, controlled segregation will reduce high-temperature oxidation.
The controlled- and disrupted-segregation variants will retain similar densities.
Exposure at 600–800 degrees Celsius represents service-relevant high-temperature oxidation conditions for aerospace and rail applications.
Ultra-rapid quenching or excessive deformation can eliminate beneficial elemental segregation and thereby terminate the proposed mechanism.
Minor-segregant concentrations above an optimum produce detrimental microstructural inhomogeneities.
